summary: Provides a framework for IP fast-reroute mechanisms that protect against link or router failure by using repair paths decided locally. Unlike MPLS fast-reroute, it works with conventional IP routing and forwarding. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IP fast-reroute lets a router use a prepared repair path when a nearby link or router fails. This can limit disruption to the time needed to detect the failure and invoke the repair.

questions: how do routers recover quickly from link failure
what is a loop free alternate
what is a micro loop in routing
subtitle: A framework for locally switching IP traffic to repair paths after a link or router failure.

tldr.problem: After a link or router fails, traffic may be lost or loop until routing converges on the new topology. This disruption can be too long for some services.
tldr.mechanism: Routers prepare repair paths in advance and the router detecting a failure switches affected traffic locally. The framework covers failure detection, repair paths, and micro-loop prevention.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a framework for IP fast-reroute, not a particular protocol. It initially focuses on link-state IGPs and leaves complete protection against multiple unrelated failures out of scope.

facts.label: Illustrative coverage with ECMP and LFA

today: RFC 5714 is an Informational RFC published in January 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides a framework, while concrete mechanisms such as loop-free alternates are specified separately.

sections.title: Why Local Repair Is Needed
sections.content:
When a link or node fails, traffic may be dropped or loop until the network re-converges. Traditionally, disruption lasted at least several seconds; carefully configured link-state IGP networks had reduced this to under a second, but some services are sensitive to shorter periods of loss.

IP fast-reroute computes backup routes so the router detecting a failure can repair traffic locally, without first informing every other router. The disruption can then be limited to failure detection and invocation of a backup route.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal routing takes time to inform routers and update forwarding tables after a failure. A locally prepared repair path can reduce how long traffic is disrupted.

sections.title: Scope and Causes of Disruption
sections.content:
The initial scope is link-state Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs), whose topology information helps routers compute repair paths. Similar mechanisms for non-link-state IGPs and BGP are left for further study. Complete protection against multiple unrelated failures is out of scope.

A conventional routing transition includes failure detection, the local router's reaction, propagation of the failure information, forwarding-table recomputation, and loading revised tables into forwarding hardware. The RFC notes that updates typically take 10 to 100 milliseconds per hop when there is no routing-protocol packet loss, while loading tables may take several hundred milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: This framework first addresses link-state routing protocols. It describes several steps between a failure and restored forwarding, including detecting the fault and updating the forwarding hardware.

sections.title: Failure Detection and Repair Paths
sections.content:
Failure detection may use physical signals such as loss of light, a routing-independent protocol such as BFD, or routing-protocol mechanisms such as fast Hellos. Packet-based detection needs care because a false failure indication can trigger an unnecessary repair.

The framework describes three basic repair-path categories: an alternate equal-cost path that avoids the failure, a loop-free alternate through a direct neighbor whose route does not return through the repairing router, or a multi-hop path through a more distant router. Multi-hop methods may use alternate forwarding tables, tunnels or loose source routes, or special addresses or labels.

The RFC gives illustrative estimates: around 80% of failures may be repaired using equal-cost paths and loop-free alternates, and around 98% by paths reaching two hops away. Actual coverage depends on topology and metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may use another equal-cost route, a neighbor's loop-free route, or a longer path through the network. The available repair options and coverage depend on the network's topology.

sections.title: Repair Coverage and Maintenance
sections.content:
Repair coverage can mean the share of links or nodes protected for every destination, destinations protected against every failure, destination-and-failure combinations protected, or normal packets that still arrive. Link protection is generally simpler than node protection. Repair paths are expected, though not required, to be pre-computed and installed for rapid use.

A repair remains in effect until routing has converged on the changed topology. Repair paths then need to be updated for future failures. Multiple unrelated failures are outside scope, and a repair path may carry enough traffic to congest its links. Operators need to know which destinations or failures cannot be protected and to monitor repair-path use.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives several ways to measure what a repair strategy protects. Operators should also know where protection is unavailable and whether repaired traffic may overload a link.

sections.title: Micro-Loops and Management
sections.content:
Temporary differences between routers' forwarding tables can create micro-loops. Looping packets can be lost and can congest links, affecting traffic that was not directly affected by the original failure. The framework describes micro-loop prevention as a possible companion to repair paths.

Management should support enabling IPFRR, configuring protection per link or node, setting repair-path preferences, configuring failure detection and loop-avoidance strategies, reporting unprotected destinations, counting repair invocations, and testing repairs.
sections.plainLanguage: During convergence, routers can briefly forward packets in a loop. Management tools should expose repair coverage and let operators configure and test the protection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework itself introduces no security issues, but proposed solutions need security review. If tunnels carry repaired traffic, their endpoints should not become an attack vector; one suggested measure is to exclude tunnel endpoint addresses from user traffic.

Some repair paths make packets arrive from a direction inconsistent with reverse path forwarding checks. Networks that rely on those checks for security need another security mechanism. Repair paths may also differ in length from the original path, which can affect security mechanisms that depend on particular TTL values.
sections.plainLanguage: Repair paths can change where packets appear to come from and how far they travel. Networks using reverse-path or TTL checks for security may need other protections.
